fetched_contents.text: A Randomized Trial of Convalescent Plasma in Covid-19 Severe Pneumonia Abstract Background Convalescent plasma is frequently administered to patients with Covid-19 and has been reported, largely on the basis of observational data, to improve clinical outcomes. Minimal data are available from adequately powered randomized, controlled trials. Methods We randomly assigned hospitalized adult patients with severe Covid-19 pneumonia in a 2:1 ratio to receive convalescent plasma or placebo. The primary outcome was the patient’s clinical status 30 days after the intervention, as measured on a six-point ordinal scale ranging from total recovery to death. Results A total of 228 patients were assigned to receive convalescent plasma and 105 to receive placebo. The median time from the onset of symptoms to enrollment in the trial was 8 days (interquartile range, 5 to 10), and hypoxemia was the most frequent severity criterion for enrollment. The infused convalescent plasma had a median titer of 1:3200 of total SARS-CoV-2 antibodies (interquartile range, 1:800 to 1:3200). No patients were lost to follow-up. At day 30 day, no significant difference was noted between the convalescent plasma group and the placebo group in the distribution of clinical outcomes according to the ordinal scale (odds ratio, 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to 1.35; P=0.46). Overall mortality was 10.96% in the convalescent plasma group and 11.43% in the placebo group, for a risk difference of −0.46 percentage points (95% CI, −7.8 to 6.8). Total SARS-CoV-2 antibody titers tended to be higher in the convalescent plasma group at day 2 after the intervention. Adverse events and serious adverse events were similar in the two groups. Conclusions No significant differences were observed in clinical status or overall mortality between patients treated with convalescent plasma and those who received placebo. (PlasmAr ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04383535.) In late 2019, the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) emerged in Wuhan, China, and has spread worldwide since then, infecting millions of people. Coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19), the disease caused by SARS-CoV-2, has clinical manifestations ranging from no symptoms to respiratory failure. So far, only two agents have shown a degree of clinical efficacy in large randomized, controlled trials: remdesivir, in hospitalized patients with pulmonary disease, and dexamethasone, in hospitalized patients receiving oxygen.1,2 Convalescent plasma has been used for the treatment of infectious diseases for more than a century, under the assumption that passive immunization can “jump start” the immune system to control the evolution of the disease until a specific immune response is established in the infected person.3 Despite great interest, convalescent plasma has been clearly demonstrated to be of value only in the treatment of Argentine hemorrhagic fever, for which it is considered standard of care.4 Although predominantly open-label, nonrandomized trials have claimed efficacy of convalescent plasma in SARS, Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), influenza A (H1N1) in 2009, avian influenza (H5N1) and Ebola, conclusive data from randomized, controlled trials are lacking.5-8 Observational studies have consistently shown that convalescent plasma has an adequate safety profile in patients with Covid-19. An exploratory analysis in 4330 patients showed no significant difference in 7-day mortality between patients who received high-titer plasma and those who received low-titer plasma in the overall population, whereas 20% lower 7-day mortality was seen in the predefined subgroup of nonintubated patients who received higher-titer plasma than in those who received lower-titer plasma (14%, vs. 11%; P=0.03). In a post hoc analysis, 7-day mortality in nonintubated patients who were younger than 80 years of age and were treated within 72 hours after diagnosis was 6.3% in those receiving high-titer plasma and 11.3% in those receiving low-titer plasma (P=0.0008).9 A similar efficacy analysis from the Mayo Clinic included 3082 participants receiving a single unit of plasma among the 35,322 patients who had received plasma through the expanded-access program.10 After adjustment for baseline characteristics, the 30-day mortality rate was 29.1% in the low-titer group and 24.7% in the high-titer group; the difference did not reach statistical significance. A post hoc subgroup analysis also suggested a benefit of high-titer plasma in patients who received plasma within 3 days after Covid-19 diagnosis. On the basis of all available data, convalescent plasma is currently available for use in the United States under an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) and has been widely used worldwide in the context of extended and compassionate use.11,12 In February 2020, the first imported case of Covid-19 was reported in Buenos Aires, and since then, the number of cases has been increasing steadily, reaching a total of more than 417,700 cases by the end of August.13 In an attempt to more clearly determine the effect of convalescent plasma in Covid-19, we planned and conducted the PlasmAr trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of convalescent plasma in the treatment of SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia. The main hypothesis of this trial was that in patients with severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia, treatment with convalescent plasma would be associated with improved clinical outcomes at 30 days. Eligible participants were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive either convalescent plasma or placebo. fetched_contents.text: Early Outpatient Treatment for Covid-19 with Convalescent Plasma Abstract Background Polyclonal convalescent plasma may be obtained from donors who have recovered from coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19). The efficacy of this plasma in preventing serious complications in outpatients with recent-onset Covid-19 is uncertain. Methods In this multicenter, double-blind, randomized, controlled trial, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of Covid-19 convalescent plasma, as compared with control plasma, in symptomatic adults (≥18 years of age) who had tested positive for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, regardless of their risk factors for disease progression or vaccination status. Participants were enrolled within 8 days after symptom onset and received a transfusion within 1 day after randomization. The primary outcome was Covid-19–related hospitalization within 28 days after transfusion. Results Participants were enrolled from June 3, 2020, through October 1, 2021. A total of 1225 participants underwent randomization, and 1181 received a transfusion. In the prespecified modified intention-to-treat analysis that included only participants who received a transfusion, the primary outcome occurred in 17 of 592 participants (2.9%) who received convalescent plasma and 37 of 589 participants (6.3%) who received control plasma (absolute risk reduction, 3.4 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, 1.0 to 5.8; P=0.005), which corresponded to a relative risk reduction of 54%. Evidence of efficacy in vaccinated participants cannot be inferred from these data because 53 of the 54 participants with Covid-19 who were hospitalized were unvaccinated and 1 participant was partially vaccinated. A total of 16 grade 3 or 4 adverse events (7 in the convalescent-plasma group and 9 in the control-plasma group) occurred in participants who were not hospitalized. Conclusions In participants with Covid-19, most of whom were unvaccinated, the administration of convalescent plasma within 9 days after the onset of symptoms reduced the risk of disease progression leading to hospitalization. (Funded by the Department of Defense and others; CSSC-004 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04373460.) In the United States, approximately 8% of persons are hospitalized after infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which causes coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19). Most therapies for Covid-19 have targeted disease progression or death in hospitalized patients. However, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued an emergency use authorization (EUA) for three monoclonal-antibody therapies for outpatients after data showed decreases in the incidences of disease progression and hospitalization when these therapies were administered within 5 to 7 days after the onset of Covid-19.1-3 Alternative outpatient therapies are needed, particularly in settings where monoclonal-antibody therapy is either unavailable (e.g., in low-income and middle-income countries),4 scarce, or ineffective (i.e., because of monoclonal antibody–resistant variants).5 Safety concerns about Covid-19 convalescent plasma have not been identified in hospitalized populations.6,7 In one study, high-titer Covid-19 convalescent plasma administered soon after hospitalization reduced the incidence of death from Covid-19 by 50%,8 but data from randomized clinical trials have not shown a consistent benefit in hospitalized patients.9 Some heterogeneity exists with respect to hospitalized participants, with some studies that show efficacy in reducing the incidence of death10,11 and others that do not show these findings.12-15 In general, improved outcomes are associated with the provision of high-titer plasma within days after the onset of symptoms.16 Data from randomized trials involving outpatients with Covid-19 are limited.17 In a trial conducted in Argentina, the use of Covid-19 convalescent plasma in outpatients was associated with a relative risk reduction of 48% in progression to severe disease (absolute risk reduction, 15 percentage points) when it was administered within 72 hours after the onset of mild Covid-19 symptoms.18 However, in a trial of Covid-19 convalescent plasma that was administered to patients in the emergency department who were at high risk for progression of Covid-19, enrollment was halted owing to futility.19 In the Convalescent Plasma to Limit SARS-CoV-2 Associated Complications (CSSC-004) Study, we sought to determine whether a transfusion of Covid-19 convalescent plasma (containing >1:320 SARS-CoV-2 anti–spike protein antibody levels) within 9 days after the onset of symptoms would be effective in preventing disease progression leading to hospitalization. Our trial population consisted of adults who were 18 years of age or older, and participants were included in the trial regardless of their coexisting conditions and vaccination status. Methods Trial Design and Oversight In this double-blind, randomized, controlled trial, we compared qualified Covid-19 convalescent plasma with control plasma. The FDA approved the trial protocol (available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org) in the investigational new drug application (IND 19725), sponsored by Johns Hopkins University. The enrollment sites and investigators are listed in the Supplementary Appendix, available at NEJM.org. Data were collected by the investigators and personnel at the blood bank at each participating site. Evidence from RCTs on safety and adverse events

The RCT evidence base is dominated by studies of hospitalized patients, with more limited outpatient and ICU-specific trials. Among the most directly relevant studies are the PlasmAr trial, a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial in hospitalized adults with severe COVID-19 pneumonia [N1-F1], and the CCAP-2 trial, a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial in hospitalized adults with COVID-19 pneumonia [N3-F3]. The outpatient setting is also represented by the CSSC-004 study, a double-blind, randomized, controlled trial of convalescent plasma in symptomatic adults who had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 within 8 days of symptom onset [N2-F2]. For ICU patients, the evidence is thinner; the provided materials mention only minimal data on use in patients with COVID-19-induced ARDS [N3-R2] and a phase II trial of convalescent plasma in moderate patients that does not appear to be ICU-focused [N5-R3].

Reported serious adverse events and related safety findings are generally modest but heterogeneous. In the PlasmAr trial, infusion-related adverse events were slightly more common in the convalescent plasma group (4.8%; 11 of 228 patients) than in the placebo group, but serious adverse events were similar between the two groups [N1-F1]. In the CCAP-2 trial, infusion-related adverse events included hypotension, rash, and respiratory distress, and no significant differences in severe adverse events or all-cause mortality were found between the intervention and placebo groups [N3-F3]. In the outpatient CSSC-004 trial, 16 grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in participants who were not hospitalized, with 7 in the convalescent plasma group and 9 in the control-plasma group [N2-F2]. These data suggest that adverse events were generally not uncommon but not clearly more frequent in the treatment arm across studies, though the outpatient trial reported a small excess of serious events in the treatment group [N2-F2].

Safety concerns did not appear to vary strongly by patient subgroup within the provided evidence, but the studies did differ in protocol design and population selection. The hospitalized trials were explicitly designed to evaluate convalescent plasma in patients with pneumonia, severe illness, or other indicators of substantial disease burden [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The outpatient study enrolled symptomatic adults within 8 days of symptom onset and assessed hospitalization as the primary outcome [N2-F2]. The ICU-specific evidence is sparse, and the provided materials indicate that data are minimal for patients with ARDS [N3-R2]. The outpatient trial also noted that safety concerns had not been identified in hospitalized populations, suggesting that adverse-event profiles may differ by setting [N2-F2].

Adverse-event monitoring and adjudication were generally rigorous in the best-studied trials. The PlasmAr trial used a double-blind design and blinded outcome adjudicators [N1-F1]. The CCAP-2 trial similarly used blinded treatment assignment and outcome adjudication, with opaque covers on intravenous lines and infusion bags [N3-F3]. The outpatient CSSC-004 trial explicitly monitored safety outcomes throughout the trial and reported grade 3 or 4 adverse events in the nonhospitalized cohort [N2-F2]. In contrast, some studies were open label or had less explicit reporting of adjudication. The provided materials also note that one pilot study was prospective, randomized, and open label [N6-R1], and another phase II open-label trial had adverse events monitored regularly [N6-R5]. Overall, the evidence suggests that safety outcomes were recorded with some consistency across trials, but the quality of event adjudication and blinding varied by study.

Overall, the RCTs collectively indicate that convalescent plasma was generally safe, with infusion-related adverse events reported but not clearly more frequent than in controls in the major blinded trials [N1-F1][N3-F3][N2-F2]. The outpatient trial reported a small excess of serious adverse events in the treatment group, but the evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous across trial populations [N2-F2]. The studies also show that safety monitoring was more systematic in larger, blinded trials, whereas open-label and smaller studies had less detailed adjudication reporting [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5].

Methodological quality and reporting standards for adverse events

Adverse events were defined and recorded in ways that varied by study, but the strongest evidence comes from the blinded trials. The PlasmAr trial explicitly defined adverse events and serious adverse events, and it reported infusion-related adverse events and serious adverse events as similar between groups [N1-F1]. The CCAP-2 trial similarly defined adverse events and serious adverse events, reporting infusion-related adverse events and noting no significant differences in severe adverse events or all-cause mortality [N3-F3]. The outpatient CSSC-004 trial reported grade 3 or 4 adverse events, with 7 in the convalescent plasma group and 9 in the control group [N2-F2]. These studies suggest that adverse events were generally classified by severity, but the exact operational definitions are not detailed in the provided excerpts.

Blinding was more consistent in the randomized controlled trials than in open-label studies. The PlasmAr trial was double-blind, with treatment assignment concealed through a randomization program and opaque covers on infusion lines and bags [N1-F1]. The CCAP-2 trial was also double-blind, with participants, clinical teams, data collectors, and outcome adjudicators blinded to treatment assignment [N3-F3]. In contrast, the outpatient CSSC-004 study did not explicitly describe a blinding scheme in the excerpt provided, but the broader context suggests that safety monitoring was routine [N2-F2]. The open-label pilot study and open-label phase II trial were less methodologically rigorous in this respect [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Adjudication was more clearly described in the blinded trials, with outcome adjudicators blinded in CCAP-2 and in PlasmAr, whereas the open-label studies do not appear to have the same level of adjudication reporting [N3-F3][N6-R1].

Safety outcomes were not uniformly prespecified. The PlasmAr trial included safety outcomes as part of its broader protocol and reported adverse events as part of the trial’s evaluation [N1-F1]. The CCAP-2 trial similarly included safety outcomes and reported them as part of the trial’s design [N3-F3]. The outpatient CSSC-004 trial explicitly monitored safety outcomes throughout the trial, but the excerpt does not clearly state whether all safety outcomes were prespecified [N2-F2]. The open-label pilot study and phase II trial were not described as prespecifying safety outcomes in the provided excerpts [N6-R1][N6-R5]. This means that post-hoc safety analysis could plausibly occur in some studies, especially in open-label designs.

Missing or unreported adverse events are likely to affect conclusions, but the evidence base is thin on this point. The provided excerpts do not give explicit details on missing events, so it is not possible to quantify the impact of missing data with confidence. However, the fact that the outpatient CSSC-004 study reported only grade 3 or 4 adverse events, while the blinded trials reported a broader set of infusion-related adverse events, suggests that event ascertainment may not be complete in all studies [N2-F2][N1-F1][N3-F3]. In addition, the open-label studies may have underreported events because they were not blinded and may not have captured all adverse events consistently [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Therefore, the evidence supports cautious interpretation of safety findings, because the quality of adverse-event recording and adjudication varied across studies [N6-R1][N3-F3][N2-F2].

Comparison of safety findings across trial populations

The safety findings differ across hospitalized, outpatient, and ICU populations, but the ICU evidence is limited. For hospitalized patients, the two major blinded trials found generally reassuring safety profiles. In the PlasmAr trial, infusion-related adverse events were slightly more common in the convalescent plasma group, but serious adverse events were similar between groups [N1-F1]. In the CCAP-2 trial, infusion-related adverse events included hypotension, rash, and respiratory distress, and no significant differences in severe adverse events or all-cause mortality were found between the intervention and placebo groups [N3-F3]. These hospitalized trials therefore suggest that convalescent plasma was generally safe, with some mild infusion-related adverse events, but not clearly more harmful than placebo.

For outpatient patients, the evidence is more mixed. The outpatient CSSC-004 trial reported 16 grade 3 or 4 adverse events in participants who were not hospitalized, with 7 in the convalescent plasma group and 9 in the control group [N2-F2]. This suggests that, in the outpatient setting, serious adverse events were small in number but still present, and the treatment group had a small excess compared with controls. The study also noted that safety concerns had not been identified in hospitalized populations, which contrasts with the outpatient finding [N2-F2]. Overall, outpatient safety appears to be somewhat more sensitive to treatment effects than hospitalized safety, at least in this trial.

The ICU-specific evidence is sparse. The provided materials indicate that minimal data are available regarding use in patients with COVID-19-induced ARDS [N3-R2]. This means that safety findings for ICU patients are not well established from the provided evidence, and any conclusions about this population should be tentative.

Adverse events were not clearly more frequent in treatment vs control arms across the hospitalized trials, but they were more common in the outpatient trial. In the hospitalized PlasmAr and CCAP-2 trials, infusion-related adverse events were reported, but serious adverse events were similar between groups [N1-F1][N3-F3]. In contrast, the outpatient trial reported a small excess of serious adverse events in the treatment arm [N2-F2]. Trial duration and follow-up also influenced safety assessment. The hospitalized trials followed patients for 30 days or more, which is important for mortality and serious adverse-event capture [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The outpatient trial followed participants for 28 days after transfusion, which is also meaningful for short-term safety, but the provided excerpts do not show that longer follow-up changed the pattern [N2-F2].

The most commonly reported adverse events across the trials were infusion-related events. The PlasmAr trial reported infusion-related adverse events [N1-F1], the CCAP-2 trial reported hypotension, rash, and respiratory distress as infusion-related adverse events [N3-F3], and the outpatient CSSC-004 trial reported grade 3 or 4 adverse events [N2-F2]. Transfusion-related serious adverse events were also specifically monitored in the outpatient trial [N2-F2]. These events were the clearest safety signals in the evidence set, whereas more severe clinical harm such as mortality or ICU admission did not consistently differ between groups in the hospitalized trials [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Overall, the safety profile appears to be more consistent across hospitalized trials, while outpatient safety showed a small but present excess of serious events [N2-F2].

What the RCT evidence says about overall safety and clinical risk

Overall, the RCT evidence suggests that convalescent plasma was generally safe but not clearly beneficial in hospitalized patients. The major blinded trials found no significant differences in clinical status, mortality, or serious adverse events compared with placebo [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The PlasmAr trial found no significant difference in clinical outcomes at day 30 and no significant mortality difference between groups [N1-F1]. The CCAP-2 trial similarly found no significant differences in severe adverse events, all-cause mortality, or clinical progression [N3-F3]. These results indicate that convalescent plasma did not show a major safety benefit or harm in hospitalized patients, and that the risk-benefit balance appears close to neutral.

Clinically significant adverse events were those that were serious or infusion-related. In the hospitalized trials, infusion-related adverse events were reported, including hypotension, rash, and respiratory distress, but these were not more frequent than in the control group in the blinded studies [N1-F1][N3-F3]. In the outpatient CSSC-004 trial, grade 3 or 4 adverse events were reported, with a small excess in the treatment group [N2-F2]. These events were considered clinically significant because they were serious and could affect treatment decisions, but they were relatively uncommon and not clearly harmful overall [N2-F2]. The broader evidence also notes that safety concerns had not been identified in hospitalized populations, suggesting that the most concerning safety signals may not be specific to hospitalized patients [N2-F2].

The evidence base has several important limitations that affect interpretation. First, the studies differed in design, blinding, and population selection. The hospitalized trials were double-blind and placebo-controlled, while the outpatient study was also double-blind but enrolled a different population [N1-F1][N3-F3][N2-F2]. Second, some studies were open label or had less explicit adjudication, which may have introduced bias [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Third, the evidence for ICU patients is very limited, so conclusions about higher-risk subgroups are tentative [N3-R2]. Fourth, safety outcomes were not uniformly prespecified, so post-hoc analysis may have influenced findings [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Finally, the provided evidence does not give strong data on missing adverse events, so conclusions about safety should be cautious [N6-R1][N3-F3][N2-F2].

The implications for clinical practice and guideline recommendations are that the RCT evidence supports a neutral safety profile for convalescent plasma, but it does not support routine use as a treatment benefit. The major guidelines and the evidence base suggest that convalescent plasma should not be used as a standard of care, and that its use should be limited to specific settings where the evidence is stronger or where the patient’s condition warrants it [N2-F2]. The outpatient study’s finding of a small excess of serious adverse events in the treatment group also suggests that clinicians should weigh the potential risks carefully, particularly in nonhospitalized patients [N2-F2]. Overall, the RCT evidence indicates that convalescent plasma is generally safe, but the clinical benefit is weak or absent, and the evidence is not strong enough to justify broad adoption [N1-F1][N3-F3][N2-F2].
